newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sues UPS for alleged discrimination.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sues UPS for alleged discrimination.

text.p: The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Thursday sued package delivery giant United Parcel Service of America Inc., alleging it violated the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The national class action lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in northern California, alleges UPS unlawfully discriminated against employees who had sight in only one eye by refusing to let them drive delivery trucks.

"We have people who have been able to drive, are cleared to drive, but yet UPS assumed that these people cannot do the job. That's a clear violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act," said William Tamayo, an attorney with the commission, a federal agency that enforces anti-discrimination laws.

Tamayo said the drivers' union had identified 40 people nationwide who could be covered by the civil suit. But the suit could extend to other people with impaired vision who may have been discouraged from applying to drive for UPS, he said.
Atlanta-based UPS, the world's largest package distribution company, said it complied with the Americans with Disabilities Act and believed the lawsuit was without merit.

"UPS believes this is a safety issue, not a disability issue. For many years, the DOT (Department of Transportation) has excluded people with monocular vision from driving commercial vehicles. UPS has adopted that safety standard for all our vehicles," it said in a statement.

However, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission said UPS had acknowledged that Department of Transportation regulations did not prohibit drivers with vision in one eye from operating vehicles weighing less than 10,000 pounds (4,500 kgs) and said that was the issue in the case.
The commission is seeking a court order to bar UPS from discriminating due to disability.
The suit seeks back pay and compensation for people allegedly hurt as well as unspecified damages.

Tamayo said the maximum damages under the Americans with Disabilities Act is back pay plus up to $300,000 for compensatory and punitive damages. He said if the courts find UPS at fault, damages could be in the millions of dollars.

Shawn Hogya, one of the UPS employees who complained to the commission, told a news conference he took a part-time job with UPS loading packages in 1990. Several years later, the company offered him the chance to become a driver.

He said he passed a driving test but when UPS found out he was partially blind in one eye "they said I have no career basically for them, that I may as well look for other work or continue to work part-time for the rest of my life."

Hogya, 26, was hit in the left eye with a baseball when he was 14, leaving him partially blind in that eye. He still works for UPS in Petaluma, Calif., and hopes the lawsuit will result in him being allowed to drive for the company.

Yvonne Harbison also complained to the commission. She was employed as a package car driver at UPS's Oakland, Calif., facility for nearly 14 years when she had an eye removed due to cancer, the commission said.

In 1994, when she asked to return to work, UPS refused to let Harbison drive smaller delivery trucks even though she was qualified, it said. She was transferred to non-driving jobs, including a position handling hazardous materials, it said.

The commission said Harbison was licensed by the California Department of Motor Vehicles to drive with vision in one eye. After Harbison complained to the commission, she was allowed to resume driving for UPS.
UPS employs about 339,000 people worldwide and provides services in 200 countries.
